name: Long bone section
summary: A wedge cut from the wall of a long bone shaft: dense compact bone built of osteons, with spongy (trabecular) bone on its inner, marrow-cavity side. One osteon is pulled out telescope-fashion to show its concentric lamellae, and the cut faces show the central and perforating canals carrying arterioles (red), venules (blue) and nerves (yellow).
clinical: Loss of bone mass thins the trabeculae of spongy bone first, because its huge surface area turns over fastest; this is why vertebral bodies, the femoral neck and the distal radius, all rich in spongy bone, are the classic fragility fracture sites.

The spaces between trabeculae hold red marrow in flat bones and the ends of long bones. Aspiration and trephine biopsy are usually taken from the posterior iliac crest, where spongy bone and red marrow persist throughout adult life.

Bone3/Mat.1.name: Compact bone
Bone3/Mat.1.description: Dense cortical bone made of osteons (Haversian systems) packed side by side. The end face shows them in cross section, each a ring of concentric lamellae around a central canal, with interstitial lamellae filling the gaps and circumferential lamellae running along the curved outer (periosteal) surface.

Bone3/Mat.5.name: Osteon
Bone3/Mat.5.description: A single osteon drawn out of the end face like a telescope to show its concentric lamellae. Collagen fibres run in a different direction in each successive lamella, which makes the osteon resist twisting; its central canal carries a small artery, vein and nerve (the coloured dots at its tip).

Bone3/Canal top.name: Central and perforating canals
Bone3/Canal top.description: Channels opened up along the cut face. Central (Haversian) canals run lengthwise through the middle of each osteon; perforating (Volkmann's) canals cross at right angles, linking central canals with each other, the periosteum and the marrow cavity.

Bone3/Cylinder.name: Central and perforating canals
Bone3/Cylinder.description: Channels opened up along the cut face. Central (Haversian) canals run lengthwise through the middle of each osteon; perforating (Volkmann's) canals cross at right angles, linking central canals with each other, the periosteum and the marrow cavity.

Bone3/Carpet.name: Spongy bone
Bone3/Carpet.description: Trabecular (cancellous) bone: a lattice of thin bony struts with no osteons, nourished by diffusion from the marrow around them. The trabeculae line up along lines of stress; in life the spaces between them are filled with red or yellow bone marrow (not modelled here).

Bone3/Bone3 part 5.name: Spongy bone
Bone3/Bone3 part 5.description: Trabecular (cancellous) bone: a lattice of thin bony struts with no osteons, nourished by diffusion from the marrow around them. The trabeculae line up along lines of stress; in life the spaces between them are filled with red or yellow bone marrow (not modelled here).

Bone3/Mat.3.name: Arterioles
Bone3/Mat.3.description: Small arteries (red = oxygenated blood) running lengthwise in the central canals and crossing between them through perforating canals. They branch from nutrient and periosteal arteries and supply the osteocytes of each osteon.

Bone3/Mat.2.name: Venules
Bone3/Mat.2.description: Small veins (blue = deoxygenated blood) that accompany the arterioles in the central and perforating canals, draining the bone back toward the periosteal and nutrient veins.

Bone3/Mat.4.name: Nerves
Bone3/Mat.4.description: Fine nerve fibres (yellow) travelling with the vessels in the central and perforating canals. Bone and especially periosteum are richly innervated, which is why fractures are so painful.

notes: No separate periosteum or marrow mesh exists: the curved outer surface is the periosteal surface of the compact bone, and the intertrabecular spaces are empty. 'Canal top' and 'Cylinder' are small textured channel surfaces on the longitudinal cut face (with short vertical stubs where perforating canals branch off); merged as 'Central and perforating canals'. 'Bone3 part 5' is white untextured geometry at the bases of the trabeculae where they meet the compact bone (mostly buried); merged into spongy bone. Arteriole/venule/nerve identities follow the red/blue/yellow colour convention. The block is a tissue sample, so no anatomical rotation applies.
